questions.lo: The varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
questions.q: Which of these shows a chemical property of an element?
options: Gallium melting in a person's hand
Iodine crystals dissolving in ethanol
Magnesium burning brightly in air
Iron and sulfur stirred together
questions.explain: Yes. Burning makes a new substance, magnesium oxide, so it shows how magnesium reacts: a chemical property.
optionWhy: You may have thought melting changes gallium into something new. In fact melted gallium is still gallium and turns solid again when cooled; its low melting point (about 30 °C) is a physical property.
You may have thought dissolving makes a new substance. In fact the iodine is only spread through the ethanol; evaporating the ethanol gives the iodine back, so this is a physical change.
Yes. Burning makes a new substance, magnesium oxide, so it shows how magnesium reacts: a chemical property.
You may have thought mixing two elements makes a new substance. In fact stirring only mixes them, and a magnet can still pull out the iron; they react only when heated.

questions.lo: The varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
questions.q: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature. All three are in Group 7. What does this show?
options: These three cannot really all be in one group
Their single atoms are a gas, a liquid and a solid
Only chlorine, as a gas, is a true non-metal
Elements in one group can be in different states
questions.explain: Yes. Elements in a group react in similar ways, but their physical properties change going down the group: here from gas to liquid to solid.
optionWhy: You may have thought elements in a group must be identical. In fact they are similar in how they react, while their states and melting points change steadily going down the group.
You may have thought each atom has the state of its element. In fact gas, liquid and solid describe a sample made of huge numbers of particles, not a single atom.
You may have thought all non-metals are gases. In fact bromine (a liquid) and iodine (a solid) are non-metals too, just like chlorine.
Yes. Elements in a group react in similar ways, but their physical properties change going down the group: here from gas to liquid to solid.

questions.lo: The varying physical and chemical properties of different elements
questions.q: The chart shows the melting points of four metals. Which statement does the chart support?
options: All four of these metals are solids at 20 °C
Two of these metals melt below 100 °C
Each of these metals has a high melting point
A single atom of iron melts at 1538 °C
questions.explain: Yes. Sodium melts at 98 °C and mercury at −39 °C, both below 100 °C. Metals' melting points vary hugely.
optionWhy: You may have thought every metal is a solid. In fact mercury melts at −39 °C, so at 20 °C it is already a liquid.
Yes. Sodium melts at 98 °C and mercury at −39 °C, both below 100 °C. Metals' melting points vary hugely.
You may have thought all metals melt only when very hot. In fact sodium melts at 98 °C and mercury at −39 °C, far lower than iron or copper.
You may have thought an atom has the properties of its element. In fact melting is something a piece of iron does; a single atom cannot melt.

questions.lo: The principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
questions.q: How did Mendeleev put the elements in order in his table?
options: By atomic mass, keeping similar elements together
By atomic number, as today's table does
By atomic mass alone, with no swaps made
By reactivity, from most to least reactive
questions.explain: Yes. Mendeleev used atomic mass for the order, but put elements with similar properties in the same group, even if that meant swapping a pair.
optionWhy: Yes. Mendeleev used atomic mass for the order, but put elements with similar properties in the same group, even if that meant swapping a pair.
You may have thought Mendeleev used today's order. In fact atomic numbers were worked out more than 40 years after his 1869 table; he used atomic mass.
You may have thought he kept strictly to mass order. In fact he swapped some pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, so that each element sat with similar elements.
You may have mixed up the periodic table with the reactivity series. In fact Mendeleev ordered the elements by atomic mass and grouped similar ones together.

questions.lo: The principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
questions.q: The diagram shows part of the periodic table with today's atomic masses. Mendeleev put tellurium (Te) before iodine (I). Why?
options: He made a mistake with their order
He was ordering by atomic number
To put iodine with chlorine and bromine
So that the two columns would look neater
questions.explain: Yes. Iodine's properties match chlorine and bromine, and tellurium's match sulfur and selenium. Mendeleev let properties decide the group, even though tellurium is heavier.
optionWhy: You may have thought any element out of mass order must be a mistake. In fact Mendeleev chose this order on purpose, so that each element sat in a group of similar elements.
You may have thought Mendeleev used atomic numbers. In fact these were not known in his time; he used atomic mass and swapped this pair because of their properties.
Yes. Iodine's properties match chlorine and bromine, and tellurium's match sulfur and selenium. Mendeleev let properties decide the group, even though tellurium is heavier.
You may have thought the layout was chosen to look tidy. In fact the swap followed the properties: iodine reacts like chlorine and bromine, not like sulfur and selenium.

questions.lo: The principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
questions.q: Mendeleev left a gap in the group with silicon and tin. What did he expect the missing element to be like?
options: Like the elements on either side in its row
Similar to silicon and tin in its group
Identical to silicon and tin in every way
Nothing could be said until it was found
questions.explain: Yes. Elements in a group have similar properties, so he predicted an element like silicon and tin. Germanium, found in 1886, matched his predictions closely.
optionWhy: You may have thought elements next to each other in a row are alike. In fact similar elements are in the same column, so he used silicon and tin to make his prediction.
Yes. Elements in a group have similar properties, so he predicted an element like silicon and tin. Germanium, found in 1886, matched his predictions closely.
You may have thought elements in a group are identical. In fact they are only similar: he predicted values, such as its atomic mass, between those of silicon and tin.
You may have thought nothing can be known about an element until it is tested. In fact the pattern of the table let Mendeleev predict its properties years before germanium was found.

questions.lo: The principles underpinning the Mendeleev periodic table
questions.q: Argon, the first noble gas to be collected, was found in 1894. Where were the noble gases in Mendeleev's first table, made in 1869?
options: In Group 0, just as in today's table
In the gaps he had left for them
At the end, as the least reactive
Nowhere: his table had no place for them
questions.explain: Yes. Mendeleev did not know a whole group was missing, so his first table had no place for the noble gases. A new group, Group 0, was added later.
optionWhy: You may have thought the periodic table has not changed since Mendeleev. In fact Group 0 was added after the noble gases were discovered.
You may have thought Mendeleev left gaps for every element found later. In fact his gaps were for a few missing elements, such as germanium; he left no space for a whole new group.
You may have thought the periodic table is a list in order of reactivity. In fact Mendeleev's table was ordered by atomic mass, and it had no noble gases at all.
Yes. Mendeleev did not know a whole group was missing, so his first table had no place for the noble gases. A new group, Group 0, was added later.

questions.lo: The periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
questions.q: In the periodic table, what is a period?
options: A row of elements going across the table
A column of elements down the table
A family of elements that react alike
A list of elements in order of reactivity
questions.explain: Yes. A period is a horizontal row. Properties change across a period, from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.
optionWhy: Yes. A period is a horizontal row. Properties change across a period, from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.
You may have mixed up the two words. A column is a group; a period is a row going across.
You may have thought the elements in a row are alike. In fact elements that react alike are in the same group (column); a period is a row.
You may have mixed up the periodic table with the reactivity series. In fact a period is simply a row of the table.

questions.lo: The periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
questions.q: The diagram shows an outline of the periodic table with one column shaded. Which statement about the shaded elements is correct?
options: They form one period of the table
They all react in a similar way
They are all gases at room temperature
They all have the same melting point
questions.explain: Yes. The shaded column is a group (Group 7), and elements in the same group react in similar ways.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up groups and periods. A column is a group; a period is a row going across.
Yes. The shaded column is a group (Group 7), and elements in the same group react in similar ways.
You may have thought all non-metals are gases. In fact this is Group 7: chlorine is a gas, but bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.
You may have thought elements in a group are identical. In fact their melting points rise going down Group 7, from gases at the top to solids lower down.

questions.lo: The periodic table: periods and groups; metals and non-metals
questions.q: What does the staircase line on the periodic table separate?
options: Metal elements from non-metals
Reactive elements from unreactive ones
Solid elements from gaseous ones
Shiny elements from dull elements
questions.explain: Yes. Metals are to the left of the staircase line and non-metals to its right. Most elements are metals.
optionWhy: Yes. Metals are to the left of the staircase line and non-metals to its right. Most elements are metals.
You may have thought only metals are reactive. In fact there are reactive and unreactive elements on both sides: fluorine and chlorine, to the right, are very reactive.
You may have thought the non-metals are all gases. In fact many non-metals to the right of the line, such as sulfur, carbon and iodine, are solids.
You may have thought being shiny decides whether an element is a metal. In fact iodine and graphite are shiny but are non-metals, to the right of the line.

questions.lo: How patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
questions.q: Potassium is below sodium in Group 1. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 7. Compared with the element above it, how reactive is each?
options: Potassium more; bromine more
Potassium less; bromine less
Potassium less; bromine more
Potassium more; bromine less
questions.explain: Yes. Going down Group 1 the metals get more reactive, so potassium beats sodium. Going down Group 7 the halogens get less reactive, so bromine is less reactive than chlorine.
optionWhy: You may have thought every group gets more reactive going down, like Group 1. In fact Group 7 goes the other way: bromine is less reactive than chlorine.
You may have thought the top element of every group is the most reactive. That is true for Group 7 but not Group 1: potassium is more reactive than sodium.
You may have swapped the two trends. Going down Group 1, reactivity increases; going down Group 7, it decreases.
Yes. Going down Group 1 the metals get more reactive, so potassium beats sodium. Going down Group 7 the halogens get less reactive, so bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

questions.lo: How patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
questions.q: Rubidium is just below potassium in Group 1. How will rubidium react with water, compared with potassium?
options: Less vigorously, as the top one reacts most
Just as vigorously, as it is in one group
More vigorously, as it is lower in the group
Unknown, as only a test can show this
questions.explain: Yes. Reactivity increases going down Group 1, so rubidium reacts even more violently than potassium, making hydrogen and an alkaline solution.
optionWhy: You may have thought the top of every group is the most reactive. In Group 1 it is the other way: reactivity increases going down.
You may have thought elements in a group react identically. In fact they react in similar ways, but reactivity changes steadily going down the group.
Yes. Reactivity increases going down Group 1, so rubidium reacts even more violently than potassium, making hydrogen and an alkaline solution.
You may have thought nothing can be said before a test. In fact the Group 1 trend lets you predict that rubidium reacts more vigorously; a test would confirm it.

questions.lo: How patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
questions.q: The diagram shows how hot iron wool reacts with three Group 7 elements. Fluorine is above chlorine. Predict how hot iron wool reacts with fluorine.
options: Less strongly than it does with iodine
Even more strongly than with chlorine
Exactly as strongly as with chlorine
Nothing can be said without a test
questions.explain: Yes. The results show reactivity falling going down Group 7, so fluorine, above chlorine, reacts most strongly of all: iron wool burns in it.
optionWhy: You may have thought every group gets more reactive going down, like Group 1. The results show the opposite for Group 7, so fluorine reacts most strongly.
Yes. The results show reactivity falling going down Group 7, so fluorine, above chlorine, reacts most strongly of all: iron wool burns in it.
You may have thought elements in a group react identically. The results show a steady change down the group, so fluorine should react even more strongly than chlorine.
You may have thought you cannot say anything before testing. In fact the trend in the results lets you predict a stronger reaction; a test would check it.

questions.lo: How patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the periodic table
questions.q: Sodium burns in chlorine. Xenon is in Group 0, below krypton. Predict what happens when sodium is heated in xenon.
options: It burns, as xenon is a gas like chlorine
It reacts, as xenon is low in its group
Unknown until someone has tested it
No reaction, as xenon is a noble gas
questions.explain: Yes. The Group 0 elements, the noble gases, hardly react at all, so sodium will not burn in xenon as it does in chlorine.
optionWhy: You may have thought elements in the same state behave alike. In fact chlorine is a reactive halogen in Group 7, while xenon is an unreactive noble gas in Group 0.
You may have thought reactivity increases going down every group. That is the Group 1 trend; the Group 0 elements hardly react at all, wherever they are in the group.
You may have thought nothing can be said before a test. In fact xenon's place in Group 0 lets you predict that it will not react.
Yes. The Group 0 elements, the noble gases, hardly react at all, so sodium will not burn in xenon as it does in chlorine.

questions.lo: The properties of metals and non-metals
questions.q: Which property do all metals have?
options: They are attracted to a magnet
They are solid at room temperature
They can conduct electricity
They have high melting points
questions.explain: Yes. Every metal conducts electricity. Most metals are solid and hard, but not all, and only a few, such as iron, are attracted to a magnet.
optionWhy: You may have thought all metals are magnetic. In fact only a few, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are; copper, aluminium and gold are not.
You may have thought every metal is a solid. In fact mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Yes. Every metal conducts electricity. Most metals are solid and hard, but not all, and only a few, such as iron, are attracted to a magnet.
You may have thought all metals melt only when very hot. In fact sodium melts at 98 °C and potassium at 64 °C.

questions.lo: The properties of metals and non-metals
questions.q: The table shows some properties of four elements. Carbon is a non-metal. Which conclusion does the table support?
options: A non-metal can still conduct electricity
Iodine is a metal, as it is shiny
Carbon must be a metal, as it conducts
Mercury is not a metal, as it is liquid
questions.explain: Yes. Carbon is a non-metal, yet graphite conducts electricity. Typical properties of non-metals have exceptions.
optionWhy: Yes. Carbon is a non-metal, yet graphite conducts electricity. Typical properties of non-metals have exceptions.
You may have thought anything shiny is a metal. In fact iodine is a non-metal in Group 7: it is shiny but does not conduct electricity.
You may have thought non-metals can never conduct. In fact carbon is a non-metal, to the right of the staircase line, and graphite still conducts.
You may have thought every metal must be solid. In fact mercury is a metal: it is shiny and conducts electricity, but it is liquid at 20 °C.

questions.lo: The properties of metals and non-metals
questions.q: Element W is dull and grey. It conducts electricity, a magnet does not attract it, and it can be hammered flat. What is W, and how can you tell?
options: A metal, as only metals conduct electricity
A non-metal, as it is dull, not shiny
A metal, as it is malleable and conducts
A non-metal, as magnets do not attract it
questions.explain: Yes. Being malleable (it can be hammered flat without breaking) and conducting electricity are typical of metals. A metal's surface often looks dull after it has reacted with the air.
optionWhy: You may have thought only metals conduct electricity. W is a metal, but not for that reason: graphite, a non-metal, conducts too. It is being malleable as well that marks W as a metal.
You may have thought one property, being dull, decides it. In fact a metal's surface often goes dull in air; W conducts and can be hammered flat, so it is a metal.
Yes. Being malleable (it can be hammered flat without breaking) and conducting electricity are typical of metals. A metal's surface often looks dull after it has reacted with the air.
You may have thought every metal is attracted to a magnet. In fact only a few metals, such as iron, nickel and cobalt, are; W is a metal that is not.

questions.lo: The chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
questions.q: Sodium oxide and calcium oxide are metal oxides that dissolve in water. What do they form?
options: An alkaline solution
An acidic solution
Just a neutral solution
Hydrogen and an alkali
questions.explain: Yes. These metal oxides are bases, and because they dissolve they make alkaline solutions, with a pH above 7.
optionWhy: Yes. These metal oxides are bases, and because they dissolve they make alkaline solutions, with a pH above 7.
You may have reversed the rule. It is non-metal oxides, such as sulfur dioxide, that make acidic solutions; metal oxides make alkaline ones.
You may have thought metal oxides are neutral. In fact these metal oxides are bases, and as they dissolve they make the water alkaline.
You may have thought the oxide reacts like the metal, giving off hydrogen. In fact no hydrogen forms: the oxide simply makes an alkaline solution.

questions.lo: The chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
questions.q: Element X burns in oxygen. Its oxide dissolves in water, making a solution of pH 3. What is X most likely to be?
options: A metal, since metal oxides are acidic
A metal, as non-metals do not burn
Either, as all oxides are acidic
A non-metal, as its oxide is acidic
questions.explain: Yes. pH 3 is acidic, and non-metal oxides, such as sulfur dioxide, make acidic solutions. X is most likely a non-metal such as sulfur.
optionWhy: You may have reversed the rule. Metal oxides that dissolve make alkaline solutions; acidic solutions come from non-metal oxides.
You may have thought non-metals are too unreactive to burn. In fact non-metals such as sulfur and carbon burn in oxygen, and their oxides make acidic solutions.
You may have thought every oxide is acidic. In fact metal oxides that dissolve make alkaline solutions, so an acidic solution points to a non-metal.
Yes. pH 3 is acidic, and non-metal oxides, such as sulfur dioxide, make acidic solutions. X is most likely a non-metal such as sulfur.

questions.lo: The chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity
questions.q: Copper oxide powder is stirred with water and filtered. The filtered water has pH 7. What is copper oxide?
options: A neutral oxide, as the water is pH 7
A base, as it can neutralise acids
An acidic oxide, like any oxide
An alkali, as it is a metal oxide
questions.explain: Yes. Copper oxide neutralises acids, for example making copper sulfate with sulfuric acid, so it is a base. It does not dissolve, so the water stays at pH 7.
optionWhy: You may have thought pH 7 shows that copper oxide is neutral. In fact it only shows that copper oxide did not dissolve; it still neutralises acids, so it is a base.
Yes. Copper oxide neutralises acids, for example making copper sulfate with sulfuric acid, so it is a base. It does not dissolve, so the water stays at pH 7.
You may have thought every oxide is acidic. In fact copper oxide is the oxide of a metal, and it neutralises acids, so it is a base.
You may have thought base and alkali mean the same. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water; copper oxide does not dissolve, so it is a base but not an alkali.
